lesson.title: The Treatment That Isn't: Understanding the Placebo
lesson.summary: A placebo is a fake treatment that looks identical to the real one but has no active ingredient, used to isolate a treatment's true chemical or physical effect from the effect of simply being treated.
lesson.body:
A placebo is a fake treatment, something that looks, tastes, or feels exactly like the real treatment being tested but contains no active ingredient and has no direct physical effect on the response being measured. A sugar pill made to look identical to a real medication, or a saline injection made to look identical to a real drug injection, are classic placebos.

Placebos exist because the act of receiving any treatment, real or fake, can change how a subject feels or behaves, simply because the subject believes something is being done for them. If researchers only compared subjects who received a real drug to subjects who received nothing at all, any improvement in the drug group could be caused by the drug itself, by the psychological experience of being treated, or by some mix of both, and there would be no way to separate the two explanations. Giving one group a placebo instead of nothing creates a comparison group that experiences the ritual and expectation of treatment without the treatment's actual chemistry, isolating whatever the chemistry itself contributes.

Suppose researchers test a new allergy medication on 200 subjects, randomly assigning 100 to receive the real medication and 100 to receive an identical looking placebo pill, with neither the subjects nor the person handing out pills told which is which. Suppose 68 of the 100 medication subjects report symptom improvement, 68%, while 41 of the 100 placebo subjects also report symptom improvement, 41%. Both numbers are nonzero, which tells you the placebo group experienced some real improvement just from participating and believing they might be treated. But the medication group's improvement rate is still 27 percentage points higher, and because assignment was random, that 27 point gap is the part of the improvement that can be attributed specifically to the medication's actual chemical effect, above and beyond whatever expecting treatment does on its own.

A placebo group typically serves as the control group in an experiment, the baseline against which every other treatment group is measured, precisely because it isolates the effect of belief and ritual from the effect of the substance itself.

Researchers typically go a step further and keep the assignment hidden from whoever administers the treatment, not just from the subjects, a practice known as double-blinding. A nurse or doctor who knows which pill is real could, entirely without meaning to, treat the two groups differently or interpret a subject's ambiguous symptoms more generously for the group they expect to improve, which would contaminate the comparison just as surely as a subject's own expectations would.

Placebos are not always usable, since it is unethical to give someone a fake treatment when withholding real treatment would cause serious harm, which is one reason some experiments compare a new treatment to the best currently available treatment instead of to a placebo. When placebos can be used, they remain one of the sharpest tools available for isolating a treatment's true effect from the psychological effect of simply being treated, a phenomenon so important it has its own name, the placebo effect, covered next.
